name: Find
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The source passage on Find deals with changelings, the fairies left behind when a child was taken. A calm baby could vanish and a cross, screaming infant appear in its place. Families found little to do but journey into Fairyland to fetch the stolen child back. Sometimes a strong glamour even led the parents to accept the changeling as their own flesh. A test could unmask the intruder. A parent might do something strange, such as beating an egg inside its shell or declaring they meant to turn eggs into beer. The changeling lost its disguise and asked what such a deed meant. Once exposed, the fairy stayed on until the true child came back from the Otherworld. Other parents left suspected changelings outside in bad weather to force a trade. In Wales people drove changelings off by cold, hunger, or water. Older folk could also be snatched when fairies had need of their skills. Midwives and musicians stood in greatest peril, along with those considered comely. Records show these beliefs sometimes excused cruelty toward children who were unwanted or weak. In the 1800s a young woman called Bridget Cleary evidently met her end by fire at the hands of her kin after falling ill, proof that the belief kept its hold.

attributes.attribute: a fairy left in place of a stolen child
detected by an unusual act such as beating an egg in its shell
revealed itself and asked the reason for the act
apparently burned to death by her family in the nineteenth century

okr.objective: Find covers changelings, fairies left where children or adults were stolen away.
key_results: A changeling replaced a stolen child, leaving a bad-tempered brat in its place.
A parent could test a changeling by an unusual act such as beating an egg inside its shell.
In Wales changelings were driven away by exposure, starvation, or drowning.
Midwives and musicians were most at risk of being stolen.
